---
title: "Stochastic actor-oriented models"
description: >
  Modelling how a network changed between observations: data, effects,
  estimation by the method of moments, convergence, and goodness of fit.
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5)
```

A stochastic actor-oriented model (SAOM; Snijders 2001; Snijders, van de
Bunt, and Steglich 2010) explains how a directed network observed at two or
more moments changed between them. The model imagines the change as a
sequence of *ministeps*: an actor gets an opportunity to change, and then
adds one outgoing tie, drops one, or leaves the network as it is, choosing
the option that leads to the network it likes best, with some randomness.
What an actor likes is an *evaluation function*, a weighted sum of
*effects* such as reciprocity, transitive closure, or similarity on a
covariate; the weights are the parameters, and the question a SAOM answers
is which tendencies, with what strength, account for the observed changes.

knappnet implements the model as RSiena defines it (Ripley et al. 2026),
with RSiena's effect definitions, covariate centering, and estimation
algorithm, and validates the deterministic parts against RSiena exactly.
This article walks through a complete analysis on a simulated panel.

```{r}
library(knappnet)
```

## A panel

`saom_data()` takes a list of directed netframes on the same actors, in
time order, plus covariates. Here the first wave is a random network on 40
actors with a binary covariate, and the later waves are generated from a
known model with `saom_simulate()`, so that we know what the estimates
should recover: a strong tendency against ties (`density` −2.2), a
preference for reciprocated ties (`recip` 1.5), transitive closure
(`transTrip` 0.3), and homophily on `smoke` (`simX` 0.6).

```{r}
set.seed(7)
n <- 40
actors <- data.frame(id = seq_len(n), smoke = rbinom(n, 1, 0.4))
ties <- which(matrix(runif(n * n) < 0.06, n, n) & !diag(n), arr.ind = TRUE)
wave1 <- netframe(data.frame(from = ties[, 1], to = ties[, 2]), nodes = actors)

model <- ~ density + recip + transTrip + simX("smoke")
truth <- c(-2.2, 1.5, 0.3, 0.6)
later <- saom_simulate(saom_data(list(wave1, wave1), covariates = "smoke"), model,
                       theta = truth, rates = 4, seed = 1)[[1]]
wave2 <- later[[1]]
later <- saom_simulate(saom_data(list(wave2, wave2), covariates = "smoke"), model,
                       theta = truth, rates = 4, seed = 2)[[1]]
wave3 <- later[[1]]

panel <- saom_data(list(wave1, wave2, wave3), covariates = "smoke")
panel
```

The covariate column `smoke` was read from the node tables; a column whose
values differ between waves becomes a changing covariate. Dyadic
covariates (matrices or netframes on the same actors) go in `dyadic`.

## Effects

Effects are written as a one-sided formula using RSiena's short names.
`saom_effects()` shows what a formula means and `saom_effect_names()`
lists what is available; the help page `?saom_effects` gives every
definition.

```{r}
saom_effects(~ density + recip + transTrip + gwespFF(parameter = 69) + simX("smoke"))
```

## Estimation

`saom_fit()` estimates the parameters by the method of moments: it looks
for parameter values under which networks simulated from each wave to the
next reproduce, on average, the observed statistics of the next wave. The
search is the three-phase Robbins-Monro algorithm of Snijders (2001) as
implemented in RSiena, and `saom_control()` holds its settings. Phase 3
is the expensive part; 1000 simulations (the default) are enough to
explore, and more are advisable for a published result. A seed makes the
result reproducible, whatever the number of threads.

```{r}
fit <- saom_fit(panel, model, control = saom_control(seed = 11, threads = 2))
fit
```

The estimates recover the generating values within their standard errors.
The last column holds the *convergence t-ratios*: for each statistic, the
mean deviation of the simulated from the observed value divided by its
standard deviation. RSiena's rule of thumb is that all of them should be
below 0.1 in absolute value and the *overall maximum convergence ratio*
(the largest t-ratio of any linear combination of the statistics) below
0.25. When that is not the case, re-estimate starting from the current
estimates:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
fit <- saom_fit(panel, model, initial = coef(fit),
                control = saom_control(seed = 12, threads = 2))
```

`summary()` adds the covariance matrix of the estimates, with correlations
below the diagonal (large correlations signal collinear effects), and the
observed and mean simulated statistics; `coef()` and `vcov()` extract the
estimates and their covariance matrix. The rate parameters say how many
opportunities for change each actor had per period; by default they are
estimated *conditionally*, from the simulated time it takes to reproduce
the observed number of changes, rather than as parameters of the
Robbins-Monro iteration (`saom_control(conditional = FALSE)` does the
latter).

```{r}
summary(fit)
```

## Estimation diagnostics

`plot()` shows the path of the parameters through phase 2. Each subphase
takes smaller steps than the one before; within a subphase the values
should wander around the final estimate rather than drift.

```{r}
plot(fit)
```

The phase 3 deviations should be centered on zero:

```{r}
plot(fit, which = "deviations")
```

## Goodness of fit

A converged model reproduces the statistics it was fitted to, by
construction. Whether it also reproduces other features of the data is the
question of goodness of fit (Lospinoso and Snijders 2019): `saom_gof()`
compares an auxiliary statistic of the observed networks (summed over the
waves after the first) with its distribution over the networks simulated
in phase 3, and reports the Mahalanobis distance of the observed value from
the simulated ones and a Monte Carlo p-value. Small p-values point to
features the model misses; here the data were generated by the model, so
the fit should be adequate.

```{r}
gof <- saom_gof(fit, "indegree")
gof
plot(gof)
```

The violins are the simulated distributions of the number of actors with
in-degree at most 0, 1, ..., 8, and the red line the observed counts.
Three other statistics are available: the out-degree distribution, the
triad census, and the distribution of geodesic distances.

```{r}
plot(saom_gof(fit, "triad_census"))
```

## What is and is not implemented

The engine covers directed one-mode networks with constant and changing
actor covariates and constant dyadic covariates; the effects in
`?saom_effects`; conditional and unconditional method-of-moments
estimation with score-function derivatives and delta-method standard
errors; simulation; and goodness of fit by auxiliary statistics. Behavior
dynamics (co-evolution of networks and actor attributes), several
dependent networks, non-directed networks, creation and endowment effects,
rate effects, missing data, structural zeros and ones, composition change,
maximum likelihood and Bayesian estimation, score-type tests, and time
heterogeneity tests are not implemented; RSiena provides all of them.
